0.0.n: Sets the time frame for the speaker’s past routine.

0.1.n: A casual personal pronoun used mainly by male speakers.

0.2.n: A vague conversational filler here, rather than a reference to a specific thing.

0.3.n: The plain form of です, used in the filler phrase あれだよ.

0.4.n: Adds emphasis to the conversational opening.

0.6.n: The name of the place the speaker regularly visited to eat.

0.7.n: Short for 通っていた, describing repeated visits in the past.

0.8.n: Follows a verb phrase to identify the time when something happened.

0.10.n: Emphasizes that the trip took a substantial amount of time.

0.11.n: A duration; 時間 counts hours rather than giving a clock time.

0.12.n: Follows an amount to make it approximate.

0.13.n: The て-form of かける links the time spent to the journey.

0.14.n: Short for 通っていた; 通う describes regularly going to the same place.

0.15.n: Short for の, adding an explanatory tone before だ.

0.16.n: Completes the explanatory んだ ending; the earlier verb carries the past tense.

0.17.n: Emphasizes this detail as information for the listener.

1.0.n: Refers to the speaker’s residence as the journey’s starting point.

1.2.n: Casually quotes 家から for confirmation with こと.

1.3.n: In ってこと？, asks whether the listener has understood the intended meaning correctly.

2.0.n: Repeats the starting point to confirm the other speaker’s question.

2.1.n: Marks the starting point; the rest of the journey description is left understood.

2.4.n: Repeating そう strengthens the enthusiastic agreement.

3.0.n: Highlights the extra effort made specifically for this visit.

3.1.n: 食べる without る combines with に行く to express the purpose of going.

3.2.n: Marks eating as the purpose of the trip.

3.3.n: Short for 行っていた, from 行く, not 行う; describes repeated past trips.

4.0.n: Points back to eating at the place just mentioned.

4.1.n: Combines with その and に to describe what the trip was for.

4.2.n: Restricts the trip’s purpose to the activity already mentioned.

4.3.n: Completes そのためだけに, marking the sole purpose of the trip.

5.0.n: A personal pronoun used mainly by male speakers.

5.1.n: Adds the speaker to the ongoing account or comparison.

5.2.n: An everyday shortening of スーパーマーケット.

5.3.n: Marks the location where the speaker worked.

5.4.n: Short for 働いていて; describes ongoing work and connects to the next part.

5.6.n: Refers back to the supermarket work just mentioned.

5.7.n: Refers here to a period of work, rather than the job overall.

5.8.n: Identifies the shift as what ended.

5.9.n: The て-form of 終わる links the shift ending to what happened afterward.

6.0.n: 急いで is the て-form of 急ぐ; it describes how the speaker goes with 行く.

6.1.n: Marks a condition that regularly led to the following result.

6.3.n: The plain past form of 間に合う, meaning arrival was early enough.

6.4.n: Short for の, presenting the result as an explanation.

6.5.n: Completes んだ; the past tense comes from 間に合った, not だ.

6.6.n: Adds emphasis to the speaker’s recollection.

6.7.n: Softens the statement and invites the listener to share the speaker’s perspective.

6.9.n: Added after the main sentence to clarify when this happened.

7.0.n: An informal acknowledgment showing the listener is following.

7.2.n: Repeated to signal continued attention and agreement.

7.4.n: Confirms agreement with what was just said.

8.0.n: Emphasizes the deliberate effort involved in making the trip.

8.1.n: Invites the listener’s attention while the speaker continues the story.

8.3.n: The name of a railway line in Tokyo.

8.5.n: The name of a railway line serving Tokyo and Chiba.

8.6.n: Marks the train line involved in the transfer with 乗り換え.

8.7.n: The connecting form of 乗り換える links changing trains with going there.

8.8.n: Short for 行っていた, from 行く, not 行う; describes a repeated past journey.

8.9.n: Short for の, adding explanation before the polite ending です.

8.10.n: Makes the explanatory ending polite; 行ってた already supplies the past tense.

8.11.n: Emphasizes the effort as a detail the listener may not have known.

0.lit: Back then, I, you know! When visiting Kururi, I regularly went, spending a good hour or so, you know.
0.tip: 通ってた is casual 通っていた, describing regular visits rather than a single trip.

1.tip: ってこと？ is a casual way to check what someone means.

2.tip: Repeating そう makes agreement sound enthusiastic and natural.

3.lit: I went out of my way to go eat!
3.tip: A verb without ます followed by に行く expresses going somewhere to do that activity.

4.tip: だけ narrows the purpose to eating there, with no other reason for the trip.

5.lit: I too was working at a supermarket, and that shift ended, and…
5.tip: Both verbs use connecting forms, keeping the story open for the next line.

6.lit: If I hurried over, I made it in time, you know! At night.
6.tip: と presents hurrying as the condition that reliably allowed the speaker to arrive in time.

7.tip: Short responses like うん show active listening without taking over the conversation.

8.lit: Out of my way, you know, Yamanote Line, Sobu Line, transferring, I used to go, you see.
8.tip: んですよ adds a polite explanatory tone, even after the casual contraction 行ってた.
